citation: Typology of market participation among smallholder farmers, Limpopo/Mpumalanga (PMC)
Commercialization of indigenous crops among smallholder farmers (Frontiers)
mechanisms: Risk aversion shaped by limited exposure to formal market systems locks out formal markets: when the familiar informal network already moves the small surplus, a new arrangement that demands technology or competitive selling is read through unfamiliarity and lack of information, not trust.

Market information is the binding constraint: without knowing grades, prices, or where to transact, a farmer cannot make a selling decision and therefore remains a price taker in whatever local outlet is available.
The harvest is mentally split into consumption first and surplus second; because the surplus is tiny, it is absorbed by the immediate community, making volume-dependent formal channels irrelevant.

Household labour is the single point of failure: when a household member's HIV-related illness withdraws a family worker, production drops to subsistence only, and any market-facing activity that needs extra hands is abandoned.

Distance is a fixed cost that eats the margin: poor roads and remoteness make the trip to a formal buyer more expensive than the gain, so the farmer defaults to the nearest informal buyer or does not sell at all.
objection_patterns: Will this require me to sell outside the people I already know?
How will I know the right price or grade without someone I trust telling me?
Do I have enough left after feeding my household to make the trip worthwhile?
Who will do the extra work if someone at home is sick?
confidence: Mixed-methods and literature synthesis, two-study triangulation, Limpopo/Mpumalanga focus — mechanisms robust for the smallholder typology, magnitudes and national prevalence unknown.
